x.ASV: A Psalm, a Song for the sabbath day. It is a good thing to give thanks unto Jehovah, And to sing praises unto thy name, O Most High;
x.Darby: A Psalm, a Song, for the Sabbath day. It is good to give thanks unto Jehovah, and to sing psalms unto thy name, O Most High;
x.KJV: A Psalm or Song for the sabbath day. It is a good thing to give thanks unto the Lord, and to sing praises unto thy name, O most High:
x.YLT: A Psalm. --A Song for the sabbath-day. Good to give thanks to Jehovah, And to sing praises to Thy name, O Most High,

nt: Here **name** represents God himself. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express this explicitly. Alternate translation: [and to sing praises to you]

x.ASV: To show forth thy lovingkindness in the morning, And thy faithfulness every night,
x.Darby: To declare thy loving-kindness in the morning, and thy faithfulness in the nights,
x.KJV: To shew forth thy lovingkindness in the morning, and thy faithfulness every night,
x.YLT: To declare in the morning Thy kindness, And Thy faithfulness in the nights.

nt: The abstract noun **covenant faithfulness** refers to God’s faithful love for the people with whom he made a covenant. If your language does not use abstract nouns, you can translate this using another form. Alternate translation: [to proclaim in the morning that you are faithful to your covenant people]

The writer is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and to proclaim your truthfulness every night]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **truthfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and that you are truthful]

x.ASV: With an instrument of ten strings, and with the psaltery; With a solemn sound upon the harp.
x.Darby: Upon an instrument of ten strings and upon the lute; upon the Higgaion with the harp.
x.KJV: Upon an instrument of ten strings, and upon the psaltery; upon the harp with a solemn sound.
x.YLT: On ten strings and on psaltery, On higgaion, with harp.

nt: A **ten string** is a kind of musical instrument with multiple strings. If your readers would not be familiar with what a ten string is, you could use the name of a similar instrument that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [an instrument with ten strings]

x.ASV: For thou, Jehovah, hast made me glad through thy work: I will triumph in the works of thy hands.
x.Darby: For thou, Jehovah, hast made me glad through thy work; I will triumph in the works of thy hands.
x.KJV: For thou, Lord, hast made me glad through thy work: I will triumph in the works of thy hands.
x.YLT: For Thou hast caused me to rejoice, O Jehovah, in Thy work, Concerning the works of Thy hands I sing.

nt: Here, **your hands** represents the capability of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of the things that you have accomplished]

x.ASV: How great are thy works, O Jehovah! Thy thoughts are very deep.
x.Darby: Jehovah, how great are thy works! Thy thoughts are very deep:
x.KJV: O Lord, how great are thy works! and thy thoughts are very deep.
x.YLT: How great have been Thy works, O Jehovah, Very deep have been Thy thoughts.

nt: Here the psalmist is speaking of God’s **thoughts** as if they were a deep pool of water because we cannot see or reach them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [Your thoughts are like a deep pool to us]

The word **thoughts** is an abstract noun that refers to what someone thinks. Some languages may not use abstract nouns. If this is true in your language, you could translate this with a verb, such as “what you think.” Alternate translation: [The things you think] or [Your plans]

x.ASV: A brutish man knoweth not; Neither doth a fool understand this:
x.Darby: A brutish man knoweth not, neither doth a fool understand it.
x.KJV: A brutish man knoweth not; neither doth a fool understand this.
x.YLT: A brutish man doth not know, And a fool understandeth not this; --

nt: אִֽישׁ־בַּ֭עַר לֹ֣א יֵדָ֑ע וּ֝⁠כְסִ֗יל לֹא־יָבִ֥ין אֶת־זֹֽאת

These two phrases **A brutish person does not know** and **a stupid one does not understand this** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [A foolish person neither knows nor understands this] or [The foolish person completely fails to understand this]

The psalmist is using the adjective **stupid** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [any stupid person]
The pronoun **this** refers to what the psalmist goes on to explain in verse 7 about wicked people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the following truth]

x.ASV: When the wicked spring as the grass, And when all the workers of iniquity do flourish; It is that they shall be destroyed for ever.
x.Darby: When the wicked spring as the grass, and when all the workers of iniquity flourish, it is that they may be destroyed for ever.
x.KJV: When the wicked spring as the grass, and when all the workers of iniquity do flourish; it is that they shall be destroyed for ever:
x.YLT: When the wicked flourish as a herb, And blossom do all workers of iniquity--For their being destroyed for ever and ever!

nt: This is a simile that speaks of wicked people appearing and growing **like grass**. Grass springs up and spreads quickly but does not last long. This emphasizes that wicked people may seem to prosper for a while, but their success will be brief. Alternate translation: [When the wicked appear quickly and seem to be everywhere as grass does]

The words **they will be destroyed** express in passive form what Yahweh will do to the wicked. If your language does not use passive forms or if the passive form would be confusing here, you can translate this with an active form. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will destroy them completely]
The pronoun **they** refers to the wicked and evildoers. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the wicked and evildoers will be destroyed]

The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [wicked people]

x.ASV: But thou, O Jehovah, art on high for evermore.
x.Darby: And thou, Jehovah, art on high for evermore.
x.KJV: But thou, Lord, art most high for evermore.
x.YLT: And Thou art high to the age, O Jehovah.

nt: The expression **are exalted** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [will live on high]

x.ASV: For, lo, thine enemies, O Jehovah, For, lo, thine enemies shall perish; All the workers of iniquity shall be scattered.
x.Darby: For lo, thine enemies, O Jehovah, for lo, thine enemies shall perish; all the workers of iniquity shall be scattered.
x.KJV: For, lo, thine enemies, O Lord, for, lo, thine enemies shall perish; all the workers of iniquity shall be scattered.
x.YLT: For, lo, Thine enemies, O Jehovah, For, lo, Thine enemies, do perish, Separate themselves do all workers of iniquity.

nt: This text uses the passive verb **will be scattered** without identifying who will do the action. The psalmist of the psalm may have written it this way to focus on what will happen to the evildoers rather than on who will scatter them. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state this in active form with God as the subject, as in the alternate translation. Alternate translation: [you will scatter all those who do evil]

x.ASV: But my horn hast thou exalted like the horn of the wild-ox: I am anointed with fresh oil.
x.Darby: But my horn shalt thou exalt like a buffalo's: I shall be anointed with fresh oil.
x.KJV: But my horn shalt thou exalt like the horn of an unicorn: I shall be anointed with fresh oil.
x.YLT: And Thou exaltest as a reem my horn, I have been anointed with fresh oil.

nt: Here, **horn** represents strength or power. The psalmist is describing how God has given him strength like that of a wild ox. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state plainly what the horn represents. Alternate translation: [But you have made me as strong as a wild ox]

Here the psalmist is speaking of himself as if he were an offering that is **saturated with fresh oil**. The abundance of oil represents God’s abundant blessing and the joy that he feels as God has made him able to defeat his enemies. Alternate translation: [you have richly blessed me] or [I am filled with joy]

x.ASV: Mine eye also hath seen my desire on mine enemies, Mine ears have heard my desire of the evil-doers that rise up against me.
x.Darby: And mine eye shall see [its desire] on mine enemies; mine ears shall hear [it] of the evil-doers that rise up against me.
x.KJV: Mine eye also shall see my desire on mine enemies, and mine ears shall hear my desire of the wicked that rise up against me.
x.YLT: And mine eye looketh on mine enemies, Of those rising up against me, The evil doers, do mine ears hear.

nt: Here **eye** and **ears** represent the whole person who sees and hears. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have seen my foes … I have heard]
וַ⁠תַּבֵּ֥ט עֵינִ֗⁠י בְּ⁠שׁ֫וּרָ֥⁠י בַּ⁠קָּמִ֖ים עָלַ֥⁠י מְרֵעִ֗ים תִּשְׁמַ֥עְנָה אָזְנָֽ⁠י

Some scholars believe that these phrases imply what it is that the writer saw and heard. You could include this information if a translation of the Bible exists in your region that includes it. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT. Alternate translation: [My eye has looked on my foes, those rising up against me, as you defeat them; those doing evil my ears have heard as you punish them]

x.ASV: The righteous shall flourish like the palm-tree: He shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon.
x.Darby: The righteous shall shoot forth like a palm-tree; he shall grow like a cedar on Lebanon.
x.KJV: The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree: he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon.
x.YLT: The righteous as a palm-tree flourisheth, As a cedar in Lebanon he groweth.

nt: The point of this comparison is that just as **the palm tree** is resilient and long-lived, so is **The righteous one**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [The righteous one will be resilient and long-lived like a palm tree]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a cedar** is strong and admired for being tall and stately, so is **The righteous one**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [he will be strong and admired like a cedar tree in Lebanon]

The psalmist is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [Any righteous person] or [All righteous people]
The pronoun **he** refers to any righteous person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [they will grow]

x.ASV: They are planted in the house of Jehovah; They shall flourish in the courts of our God.
x.Darby: Those that are planted in the house of Jehovah shall flourish in the courts of ourGod:
x.KJV: Those that be planted in the house of the Lord shall flourish in the courts of our God.
x.YLT: Those planted in the house of Jehovah, In the courts of our God do flourish.

nt: The psalmist uses the passive verb **are planted** and does not tell who has done the planting. You may need to state clearly who did the planting if your language does not use passive verbs in this way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has planted them] or [Yahweh takes care of them as if they were trees that he had planted]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if righteous people were actually **planted** trees growing in Yahweh’s house. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [they flourish like trees] or [they live securely]

The pronoun **They** refers to righteous people, who are those who are planted in Yahweh’s house. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Righteous people are planted]

Here the psalmist is speaking of righteous people as if they were plants that **flourish**, which means that they are strong and healthy. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this image differently or state this plainly without the image. Alternate translation: [they grow well] or [they prosper]

x.ASV: They shall still bring forth fruit in old age; They shall be full of sap and green:
x.Darby: They are still vigorous in old age, they are full of sap and green;
x.KJV: They shall still bring forth fruit in old age; they shall be fat and flourishing;
x.YLT: Still they bring forth in old age, Fat and flourishing are they,

nt: The psalmist is speaking of people who are faithful to God as if they were **fruit**-bearing trees. This image emphasizes how they continue to be productive and do good things. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They continue doing good things]
The pronoun **They** continues to refer to righteous people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Righteous people, like trees, bear fruit]

Here the psalmist speaks of **juicy and green** as if the righteous people were plants that are healthy and full of life. This metaphor compares their spiritual and physical well-being to the freshness of a flourishing plant. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state plainly what this means. Alternate translation: [they remain strong and healthy] or [they always do what pleases God]

x.ASV: To show that Jehovah is upright; He is my rock, and there is no unrighteousness in him.
x.Darby: To shew that Jehovah is upright: [he is] my rock, and there is no unrighteousness in him.
x.KJV: To shew that the Lord is upright: he is my rock, and there is no unrighteousness in him.
x.YLT: To declare that upright is Jehovah my rock, And there is no perverseness in Him!

nt: If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [showing that] or [which shows that]

Here the psalmist speaks of Yahweh as if he were a **rock**, because a large rock can provide protection and safety. You could keep this image in your translation if it is clear, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this in [Psalm 18:2](../018/002.md). Alternate translation: [the one who protects me]

Here the psalmist is speaking of **unrighteousness** as if it were a substance or object that could be present in or absent from someone. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he is always righteousness]

The phrase **no unrighteousness** uses two negative words to express a positive meaning. The psalmist is saying that God is completely righteous. If your language does not use double negatives, you could express this with a positive statement. Alternate translation: [and he is always righteousness]
